entities.summary:
Jean d'Orléans-Longueville was a cardinal of the Roman Catholic Church who played a pivotal role in shaping the religious landscape of 16th-century Europe. Born in France, Longueville rose to prominence as a member of the powerful House of Orléans and was appointed Archbishop of Toulouse in 1503. Two years later, he became Bishop of Orléans, a position he held until his death in 1533.

As Cardinal, Longueville participated in several high-stakes religious councils, including the 1533 Council of Trent, where he advocated for a more conservative approach to reform. His involvement in the council helped to solidify the Catholic Church's stance on issues such as clerical celibacy and the role of the Pope.

Despite his significant contributions to the Church, Longueville's tenure as Cardinal was marked by controversy and power struggles. His appointment to the See of Toulouse was met with resistance from other powerful clergy, and his influence was eventually eclipsed by that of other prominent cardinals.

In the aftermath of his death, Longueville's legacy continued to shape the religious landscape of Europe. His commitment to conservative reform and his role in shaping the Council of Trent had a lasting impact on the development of Catholic doctrine and practice.

"The Church is the pillar and foundation of true religion," Longueville once said, "and its authority must be respected and upheld." These words, spoken during his time as Cardinal, continue to resonate with Catholics around the world today.

Jean d'Orléans-Longueville, Cardinal de Longueville, was a cardinal of the Roman Catholic Church for six months in 1533. He was a prominent figure in the French clergy and played a key role in the religious and political landscape of 16th-century France. Born in 1484 at the Château de Parthenay, he went on to become the abbot in commendam of Bec and concurrently the archbishop of Toulouse (1503) and bishop of Orléans (1521).

He was a member of the powerful Orléans-Longueville family and was known for his conservative religious views. His appointment as cardinal was seen as a way to consolidate the family's influence in French politics.

Despite his relatively short tenure as cardinal, Longueville's legacy continued to shape the French Catholic Church and the country's religious landscape for generations to come.

The cardinal's life was marked by tragedy, including the loss of his daughter and the tumultuous events of the French Wars of Religion.

In the end, Longueville's contributions to the French Catholic Church and his role in shaping the country's religious landscape make him a significant figure in French history.
